Copper rockfish (Sebastes caurinus) is a viviparous scorpaenid that inhabits nearshore rocky reefs and kelp forests along the northeastern Pacific coast. Fertilisation is internal, and females give birth to active, yolk-sac larvae following a gestation period that is strongly influenced by temperature. In this species, the dry mass of a newly released larva is remarkably small, with each individual weighing only 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] at the moment of parturition. This minute initial size reflects the constraints of producing thousands of offspring simultaneously, as the female must allocate resources across a large brood before the onset of exogenous feeding. As the yolk-sac larva begins to absorb its endogenous reserves, it undergoes a trophic switch that marks the transition to active feeding. The pelagic larval phase is brief compared to many marine teleosts, and larval metamorphosis involves a pronounced allometric shift as the fish settles into a demersal habitat. Growth during the first year is rapid, driven by the high productivity of adjacent foraging grounds.

Body size at the onset of sexual maturation is a key life-history parameter for this commercially important species. Field surveys indicate that puberty, defined by the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes or spermatogenic cysts in the gonads, is attained at a total length of 34 centimeters [Lp = 34 centimeters]. This threshold is associated with a corresponding body mass of 540 grams [Wwp = 540 grams] for the average individual at the time of reproductive activation. The allometric relationship between length and wet weight for maturing fish follows a typical power function derived from extensive field sampling of the population. Individuals below this size class are almost invariably immature, and the onset of gametogenesis appears to be tightly linked to reaching this critical length rather than strictly to chronological age. The reproductive strategy of this species is characterized by a protracted spawning season and iteroparity, with females producing a single brood annually once maturity has been achieved. Annual fecundity scales positively with female body size, ensuring that larger, older females contribute disproportionately to recruitment.

Under the stable thermal conditions of 8.3 °C [T = 8.3 °C], which reflect the average annual water temperature in the deeper portions of this species' depth range, reproductive output is substantial. Females produce approximately 640,000 offspring per brood [N_R_i = approximately 640,000 offspring per brood], with a single brood each year [F_R_i = single brood each year]. This remarkable fecundity is facilitated by the large body cavity and the efficient packing of small, yolk-laden eggs within the ovary prior to internal fertilisation. The developing embryos rely entirely on maternally derived yolk for their nutrition throughout gestation. The temperature dependency of gestation length is notable, as colder waters prolong the developmental period and may delay parturition by several weeks compared to warmer inshore environments. Such thermal sensitivity has implications for the timing of larval release relative to peak zooplankton abundance, a critical match-mismatch dynamic that influences early survival. Management strategies must account for this high reproductive potential when setting harvest limits.

The ultimate body size that this species can achieve under favorable conditions places it among the larger members of the genus Sebastes. The maximum total length recorded for Copper rockfish is 58 centimeters [Li = 58 centimeters], a metric that represents the asymptotic size approached by the oldest and largest individuals in the population. This length corresponds to a maximum adult wet weight of 2,800 grams (2800 grams) [Wwi = 2800 grams], derived from the robust, deep-bodied morphology typical of demersal rockfish. These large adults are commonly found in structurally complex habitats such as boulder fields and rock pinnacles, where they can find refuge from predators and access to diverse prey. The slow growth rate and extended reproductive lifespan of this species mean that the largest individuals are likely several decades old. Their contribution to the spawning stock is disproportionately important, as fecundity increases markedly with size. Protecting these large, old individuals is therefore a priority for maintaining the resilience of the population.

Longevity is a defining feature of the life history of Copper rockfish, which is consistent with the general pattern observed in the genus Sebastes. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species under natural conditions is approximately 57 years [am = approximately 57 years], as determined from otolith annulus counts in water temperatures averaging 8.3 °C [T = 8.3 °C]. This extreme longevity, unusual among teleosts, is accompanied by a slow rate of senescence and the ability to maintain reproductive competence well into advanced age. The stable, cold thermal regime of their preferred deep-reef environment likely contributes to reduced metabolic rates and cumulative oxidative damage over time. The oldest individuals are most vulnerable to fishing pressure, which selectively removes the largest and most fecund members of the population. Consequently, size-selective harvest can erode the age structure of the population, reducing its capacity to withstand environmental variability. Effective conservation requires management measures that protect the age diversity of the spawning stock.
